summary.text: For the counterexample $n=800322180$, monotonicity of $B(k)=\binom{2k+1}{k}$ and $B(16)=1166803110>n$ force $0\le c\le d\le15$. A finite check of these 136 pairs shows that every residual $n-B(c)-B(d)$ contains a prime $p\equiv3\pmod4$ to an odd exponent, so the sum-of-two-squares criterion rules out every possible representation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
B(k)=\binom{2k+1}{k}.
\]
We will show that
\[
N=800322180
\]
has no representation
\[
N=a^2+b^2+B(c)+B(d)
\]
with nonnegative integers \(a,b,c,d\), even before the conditions \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\) are taken into account except that \(c\le d\) lets us shorten the finite case analysis. Since \(N>1\), this gives a counterexample to the conjecture.

We first recall the elementary obstruction for a number to be a sum of two squares.

**Sum-of-two-squares obstruction.** Suppose \(q\) is a prime with \(q\equiv3\pmod4\). If
\[
x^2+y^2=M,
\]
then the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of \(M\) is even. In particular, if \(q\) divides \(M\) to an odd exact exponent, then \(M\) is not a sum of two integer squares.

Here is a proof sufficient for what follows. If \(q\mid x^2+y^2\), then reduction modulo \(q\) gives
\[
x^2+y^2\equiv0\pmod q.
\]
If \(y\not\equiv0\pmod q\), division by \(y^2\) would show that \((xy^{-1})^2\equiv-1\pmod q\). But \(-1\) is not a quadratic residue modulo a prime \(q\equiv3\pmod4\): if \(t^2\equiv-1\pmod q\), then
\[
t^{q-1}=(t^2)^{(q-1)/2}\equiv(-1)^{(q-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod q,
\]
whereas Fermat's theorem gives \(t^{q-1}\equiv1\pmod q\). Thus \(y\equiv0\pmod q\), and then also \(x\equiv0\pmod q\). Consequently \(q\mid x\) and \(q\mid y\), so \(q^2\mid x^2+y^2\), and after writing \(x=qx_1\), \(y=qy_1\), we obtain
\[
M=q^2(x_1^2+y_1^2).
\]
Repeating this argument shows that every occurrence of \(q\) in \(M\) is removed in pairs. Its exact exponent must therefore be even.

We next reduce the possible binomial indices to a small finite range. From the factorial formula,
\[
\frac{B(k+1)}{B(k)}
 =\frac{\binom{2k+3}{k+1}}{\binom{2k+1}{k}}
 =\frac{(2k+3)(2k+2)}{(k+1)(k+2)}
 =\frac{2(2k+3)}{k+2}>1.
\]
Thus \(B(k)\) is increasing. Direct evaluation gives
\[
B(16)=\binom{33}{16}=1166803110>N.
\]
If a representation of \(N\) existed and \(d\ge16\), then its nonnegative summand \(B(d)\) would already exceed \(N\), which is impossible. Hence \(d\le15\). Under the required ordering \(c\le d\), this also gives \(c\le15\).

The needed binomial values are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
B(k)&1&3&10&35&126&462&1716&6435
\end{array}
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&8&9&10&11&12&13&14&15\\ \hline
B(k)&24310&92378&352716&1352078&5200300&20058300&77558760&300540195.
\end{array}
\]
These values follow successively either from the factorial formula or from the ratio above.

It remains to consider every pair \(0\le c\le d\le15\). For such a pair, a putative representation would require
\[
a^2+b^2=R_{c,d}:=N-B(c)-B(d).
\]
The following table supplies, for every one of the \(136\) possible pairs, a prime obstruction. An entry
\[
d:q^e
\]
in row \(c\) means that \(q\equiv3\pmod4\) is prime and that \(q^e\) exactly divides \(R_{c,d}\), with \(e\) odd. When the exponent is \(1\), it is omitted. Thus each entry contradicts the sum-of-two-squares obstruction proved above.

\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
c&\text{entries }d:q^e\\ \hline
0&0:647,\ 1:163,\ 2:67,\ 3:3,\ 4:23,\ 5:467,\ 6:223,\ 7:991,\\
 &8:7,\ 9:3,\ 10:23,\ 11:3,\ 12:887,\ 13:26905651,\ 14:7,\ 15:1999\\[2pt]
1&1:3^3,\ 2:643,\ 3:19,\ 4:3,\ 5:3^7,\ 6:3,\ 7:3,\ 8:78607,\\

3&3:7,\ 4:7,\ 5:7,\ 6:43,\ 7:5843,\ 8:3,\ 9:7923067,\ 10:7,\\

8&8:689891,\ 9:3,\ 10:223,\ 11:3,\ 12:59,\ 13:11,\ 14:7591,\ 15:19990307\\[2pt]
9&9:19,\ 10:887,\ 11:19,\ 12:3,\ 13:11,\ 14:19,\ 15:19\\[2pt]
10&10:3,\ 11:19,\ 12:7,\ 13:19,\ 14:3^3,\ 15:19\\[2pt]
11&11:7,\ 12:3,\ 13:19,\ 14:19,\ 15:19\\[2pt]
12&12:7,\ 13:19,\ 14:19,\ 15:19\\[2pt]

\end{array}
\]

For completeness, this table is a direct finite divisibility computation, not an appeal to the full sum-of-two-squares characterization. For each entry one first forms \(R_{c,d}=800322180-B(c)-B(d)\) using the displayed binomial table, divides it by the displayed power \(q^e\), and checks that the resulting quotient is not divisible by \(q\). The displayed primes are all congruent to \(3\) modulo \(4\). Their primality is checked by trial division: for each displayed \(q\), no prime at most \(\sqrt q\) divides it. Since any composite integer has a prime divisor at most its square root, this establishes the asserted primality. Thus the table records exact odd valuations, which is precisely the information needed in the obstruction lemma.

To illustrate both an ordinary entry and why the entries with higher powers are handled correctly, consider the first pair \((c,d)=(0,0)\). Here
\[
R_{0,0}=800322180-1-1=800322178.
\]
The table says that \(647\), a prime congruent to \(3\pmod4\), divides this number but \(647^2\) does not. Therefore \(R_{0,0}\) cannot be a sum of two squares. For the pair \((1,1)\),
\[
R_{1,1}=800322180-3-3=800322174=3^2\cdot88924686,
\]
and \(88924686\) is divisible by \(3\) but not by \(9\). Hence the exact exponent of \(3\) in \(R_{1,1}\) is \(3\), still odd. If \(R_{1,1}=a^2+b^2\), the divisibility lemma would force \(3\mid a,b\), and dividing both squares by \(3^2\) would leave a sum of two squares divisible by \(3\) but not \(9\), an impossibility. The entries \(3^5\) and \(3^7\) work in exactly the same way: repeatedly divide both putative square roots by \(3\), removing two factors of \(3\) at each stage, until one factor of \(3\) remains. This explicitly accounts for every exceptional higher-valuation case in the table.

Now suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(N\) had a representation of the required form. As shown above, its ordered indices would satisfy \(0\le c\le d\le15\). Locate that pair in the table. The corresponding entry gives a prime \(q\equiv3\pmod4\) whose exact exponent in
\[
R_{c,d}=N-B(c)-B(d)=a^2+b^2
\]
is odd. This contradicts the sum-of-two-squares obstruction. Hence no such representation exists. The inequalities \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\) cannot rescue a representation; indeed, we have ruled out a sum of two squares for every ordered binomial pair, irrespective of the order of \(a,b\).

Therefore the number of representations of \(800322180\) as
\[
a^2+b^2+\binom{2c+1}{c}+\binom{2d+1}{d},
\qquad a\le b,\quad c\le d,
\]
is zero. Since \(800322180>1\), the assertion that this number is positive for every \(n>1\) is false.
